newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seeks details on NATO-Russia deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks details on NATO-Russia deal.

text.p: The United States is pleased that NATO and Russia agreed on a deal to forge a peaceful new relationship but wants to hear details before giving a definitive reaction, a senior U.S. official said on Wednesday.

NATO Secretary General Javier Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov "had a very good meeting today (in Moscow) and appear to have cleared away the obstacles toward an agreement ... (but) we need to get briefed by Solana and see the documents before we can react much further," he said.

The U.S. official, who spoke anonymously, said he understood Solana was enroute to Brussels and would brief NATO's political arm, the North Atlantic Council, at alliance headquarters in several hours.
"He left Moscow and we didn't have a chance to talk to him so we don't know the substance" of the final agreement, reached after two days of talks in Moscow between Solana and Primakov, he said.
President Bill Clinton or Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was expected to provide the official U.S. reaction when the administration was prepared to do that later in the day.
The announcement of the deal came in a joint statement from Moscow. Details of the accord were not immediately released and it was not clear if all differences had been fully resolved.

A breakthrough had been blocked until now by disagreements over whether the pact should include written guarantees that NATO will not station military structures and nuclear weapons on the territory of new member states. The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation has been reluctant to give such guarantees in writing.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin has made clear he wants to sign an agreement with NATO on May 27 in Paris and said last week the deal was "98 percent" ready. U.S. officials said on Tuesday the NATO-Russia talks were at a crucial point and if Solana and Primakov could not reach agreement on Wednesday, the May 27 event might have to be postponed.

The NATO-Russia agreement was conceived as a way to forge closer ties between the alliance and its former enemy at the same time that NATO was planning to accept former Soviet bloc states as new members.

Moscow strongly opposes NATO expansion but agreed to negotiate a new relationship with the alliance that would create a formal joint cooperation council and give Russia a voice but no veto in NATO decision-making on European security.

Leaders of the 16 NATO countries meet in Madrid on July 8-9 to decide the alliance's first new members of the post-Cold War era. Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic are considered certain but Romaina and Slovenia are also being discussed.
